subject: Financial Literacy
chapter: Compound Interest & The Power of Time
title: Aisha's ₹10,000 Journey to ₹1 Lakh
hook: How can a young girl turn ₹10,000 into ₹1 lakh without working extra? The power of compound interest.

characters.name: Aisha
characters.role: A 13-year-old student who saves her pocket money

characters.name: Grandma
characters.role: Aisha's grandmother who taught her about long-term investing

characters.name: Mr. Sharma
characters.role: Bank manager who explains fixed deposits and compound interest

slides.title: Compound Interest & The Power of Time
slides.storyContext: Aisha receives ₹10,000 from her grandmother on her 13th birthday. 'If you invest this wisely,' Grandma says, 'it will grow without you lifting a finger. Let me show you how.'

image.alt: Compound Interest & The Power of Time — Compound Interest & The Power of Time

slides.title: The Magic of Waiting
slides.storyContext: Aisha's grandmother invites her to the bank. Mr. Sharma, the bank manager, greets them warmly. 'Your grandmother is right. Money has a hidden power—it can earn money on top of its own money. We call this compound interest. It's like planting a seed that grows leaves, and those leaves grow more seeds.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Money you save in a bank doesn't just sit there—it grows over time, earning interest on interest.

image.alt: The Magic of Waiting — Compound Interest & The Power of Time

slides.title: What is Interest? Money Earns More Money
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma explains: 'When you deposit money in a bank, we use it to lend to people and businesses. We pay YOU a portion of what we earn—that's interest. Think of it as rent we pay for borrowing your money.'

points.label: Interest
points.text: Money the bank pays you for letting them use your money.

points.label: Interest rate
points.text: Expressed as a percentage per year (% per annum). Example: 8% per annum means ₹8 for every ₹100 saved.

points.label: Aisha's example
points.text: ₹10,000 at 8% per annum = ₹800 interest in year 1.

slides.inSimpleWords: Interest is free money the bank gives you for savings. The higher the rate, the more you earn.

slides.title: Simple Interest vs. Compound Interest
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma draws two paths. 'Simple interest is like this: I give you ₹100 and 10% interest every year. Year 1: you get ₹10. Year 2: you get ₹10 again. Always ₹10. Boring, right? But compound interest is different. Year 1: you get ₹10 on ₹100. Year 2: you get interest on ₹110. Year 3: on ₹121. It keeps growing!'

points.label: Simple Interest
points.text: Interest is calculated only on the original amount (Principal). Formula: SI = (P × R × T) ÷ 100

points.label: Compound Interest
points.text: Interest is calculated on Principal + Previous Interest. Each year, the amount earning interest grows.

points.label: Key Difference
points.text: Simple interest is flat. Compound interest accelerates—interest earns interest, creating exponential growth.

example.problem: ₹1,000 at 10% per annum for 2 years. Compare simple and compound interest.
example.solution: Simple Interest: SI = (1000 × 10 × 2) ÷ 100 = ₹200. Amount = ₹1,200. Compound Interest: Year 1: ₹1,000 + ₹100 = ₹1,100. Year 2: ₹1,100 + ₹110 = ₹1,210. Difference: ₹10 (compound is bigger).

slides.inSimpleWords: With compound interest, your money grows faster because interest itself starts earning interest.

image.alt: Simple Interest vs. Compound Interest — Compound Interest & The Power of Time

slides.title: Year 1: The First Interest Arrives
slides.storyContext: Aisha deposits ₹10,000 on January 1st. Mr. Sharma says: 'We offer 8% per annum on fixed deposits. By December 31st, you'll get interest.' Aisha asks, 'How much?' Mr. Sharma: '8% of ₹10,000 = ₹800. So you'll have ₹10,800.' Aisha's eyes widen. 'I earned ₹800 without doing anything!' Her Grandma: 'Yes, beta. Now imagine if you left that ₹10,800 to grow for another year...'
slides.inSimpleWords: Aisha's first year: ₹10,000 earns 8% interest = ₹800 gained. New balance: ₹10,800.

slides.title: The Compound Interest Formula
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma writes on the whiteboard: **A = P(1 + r/100)^t**. 'This formula tells you how much money you'll have after t years. P is your starting money (Principal), r is the interest rate, and t is time in years.'

points.label: A
points.text: Final Amount (money you have after interest)

points.label: P
points.text: Principal (money you start with)

points.label: r
points.text: Rate of interest per annum (% per year)

points.label: t
points.text: Time in years

points.label: Remember
points.text: Compound Interest = A − P (the gain)

example.problem: Aisha invests ₹10,000 at 8% per annum for 3 years. How much will she have?

slides.inSimpleWords: Use A = P(1 + r/100)^t to find your final amount. The longer you wait, the bigger the multiplier.

image.alt: The Compound Interest Formula — Compound Interest & The Power of Time

slides.title: Year by Year: Watching the Magic Work
slides.storyContext: Aisha creates a spreadsheet with Grandma. 'Let's see what happens year by year, beta.' They calculate each year using compound interest.

example.problem: Aisha's ₹10,000 at 8% per annum. Calculate the balance for years 1–5.

slides.title: Time is Your Superpower
slides.storyContext: Grandma holds Aisha's hand. 'The secret is time. If you invest ₹10,000 today at age 13 and leave it untouched until you're 30, even at 7% interest, you'll have over ₹70,000. That's not your hard work—that's the power of time doing the work for you.'

points.label: Early Start
points.text: Start investing young. Even small amounts grow huge over 20–30 years.

points.label: Compound Growth
points.text: 10 years: 2× growth. 20 years: 3–4× growth. 30 years: 5–10× growth (depending on interest rate).

points.label: Real Example
points.text: ₹10,000 at 10% per annum: After 10 years = ₹25,937. After 20 years = ₹67,275. After 30 years = ₹174,494.

example.problem: Aman starts with ₹5,000 at age 20 at 9% per annum. By age 50 (30 years), how much will he have?

slides.inSimpleWords: Start young. Even if you invest just a little, 20–30 years of compound interest will turn it into a fortune.

image.alt: Time is Your Superpower — Compound Interest & The Power of Time

slides.title: Aisha Meets Her Friend Who Waits
slides.storyContext: Aisha tells her friend Rohan: 'I'm investing ₹10,000 now at 8%.' Rohan says: 'That's great, but I can't start. I'll invest ₹20,000 when I'm 25 (in 12 years).' Aisha: 'Let's see who wins!' Grandma smiles mysteriously. 'You both will—but Aisha has a secret advantage.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Aisha starts early with ₹10,000. Rohan waits 12 years but invests ₹20,000. Who ends up with more at age 43?

slides.title: The 72 Rule: Quick Mental Math
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma teaches a shortcut: 'Divide 72 by your interest rate to estimate doubling time.' Aisha: '72 ÷ 8 = 9. So my money doubles every 9 years?' Mr. Sharma: 'Roughly, yes! It's an approximation but very useful for quick estimates.'

points.label: Rule of 72
points.text: Doubling time ≈ 72 ÷ interest rate (%). At 8%, money doubles in ~9 years.

points.label: Verification
points.text: ₹10,000 at 8% for 9 years: 10,000 × (1.08)^9 = ₹21,589. Actually ₹21,589, close to double.

points.label: Why useful?
points.text: Quickly estimate wealth growth without a calculator. At 5%, doubles every 14.4 years. At 10%, every 7.2 years.

slides.inSimpleWords: The Rule of 72 is a quick mental trick: divide 72 by the interest rate to find roughly how long until your money doubles.

slides.title: Aisha's Milestone: From ₹10K to ₹20K
slides.storyContext: At age 22 (9 years later), Aisha checks her statement: ₹21,589. She's hit the 2× milestone! Grandma: 'This is your second doubling point. From here, the next doubling will be just as fast.' Aisha realizes: 'My money will keep doubling every 9 years. By 43, I'll have 4 doublings... that's ₹10,000 × 16... ₹160,000!'
slides.inSimpleWords: At year 9, Aisha's ₹10,000 doubles to ₹21,589. The magic is that each doubling takes roughly the same time.

slides.title: The Trap: Lifestyle Inflation
slides.storyContext: Year 10: Aisha gets a job and her income rises. She's tempted to spend more. Grandma warns: 'Many rich people end up poor because they inflate their spending as income grows. Keep investing a percentage of your new income. Let wealth snowball.' Aisha: 'You mean I should invest ₹1,000 MORE every year?' Grandma: 'Exactly. Your growth will accelerate.'
slides.inSimpleWords: As Aisha earns more, she resists the urge to inflate spending. She invests extra money too, speeding up compound growth.

slides.title: Additional Investments Amplify Growth
slides.storyContext: If Aisha adds ₹1,000 every year (year 1–30) in addition to her initial ₹10,000, her final balance is MUCH higher.

points.label: With annual ₹1,000 additions
points.text: ₹10,000 + (₹1,000 × 30 years) at 8% compound = ₹1,50,000+ (rough estimate).

points.label: The power
points.text: Regular additions + compound interest on those additions = exponential acceleration.

slides.inSimpleWords: When you add extra money to your investment regularly, compound interest works on those additions too. Growth accelerates dramatically.

slides.title: Aisha's Aggressive Saving Plan
slides.storyContext: At age 30, Aisha decides: 'I'll invest ₹5,000 every year (from salary) for the next 13 years until age 43.' How much extra will this add to her wealth compared to no additional saving?

example.problem: Aisha's original ₹10,000 (now 17 years invested, ₹37,386). She adds ₹5,000 every year for 13 years at 8% compound. By year 30, how much total?
example.solution: Original ₹10,000 after 30 years = ₹1,00,626. Additional savings (₹5,000 × 13 years) with compound: roughly ₹80,000. Total ≈ ₹1,80,000. The extra ₹65,000 invested added ₹80,000 of wealth. Compound interest on those additions = ₹15,000 free money.

slides.title: Aisha at 43: The Outcome
slides.storyContext: Aisha's final check at age 43: Original ₹10,000 invested at 8% for 30 years = ₹1,00,626. Additional ₹5,000/year for 13 years (from age 30–43) compounded = ₹80,000. Total: ₹1,80,626. She's exceeded her ₹1 lakh goal by 80%! Grandma hugs her. 'Beta, you started young, compounded smartly, and added to your investments. You're living proof that compound interest works.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Aisha's final wealth at 43: ₹1,80,626. She invested ₹10,000 initially + ₹65,000 extra = ₹75,000 total out of pocket. The extra ₹1,05,626 is pure compound interest magic.

slides.title: Interest Rates & Where to Invest
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma shows Aisha options. 'Different places offer different interest rates. A savings account gives 4% per year. A fixed deposit at the bank gives 7–8%. Government bonds give 5–6%. Choose based on how much risk you can handle and how long you can wait.'

points.label: Savings Account
points.text: Safest, lowest returns (4–5% per annum). Money is liquid (easy to withdraw).

points.label: Fixed Deposit (FD)
points.text: Safe, medium returns (7–8% per annum). Money is locked for a fixed period (1–5 years).

points.label: Government Savings Schemes
points.text: Very safe, decent returns (5–7% per annum). Examples: NSC, Post Office RD.

points.label: Rule of Thumb
points.text: Higher return = higher risk. Start with safe options like FDs.

example.problem: Compare: ₹10,000 at 5% (savings account) vs. ₹10,000 at 8% (fixed deposit) for 10 years.
example.solution: At 5%: A = 10,000(1.05)^10 = ₹16,288.95. At 8%: A = 10,000(1.08)^10 = ₹21,589.25. The FD earns ₹5,300 MORE just because the rate is higher!

slides.inSimpleWords: Different savings options offer different interest rates. A higher rate means your money grows faster.

image.alt: Interest Rates & Where to Invest — Compound Interest & The Power of Time

slides.title: The Rate Matters: 8% vs. 10% Over 30 Years
slides.storyContext: Aisha wonders: 'If I find an 8% fixed deposit vs. a 10% scheme, does 2% extra really matter over 30 years?' Let's do the maths.

example.problem: ₹10,000 invested for 30 years: at 8% per annum vs. 10% per annum. What's the difference?
example.solution: At 8%: A = 10,000(1.08)^30 = 10,000 × 10.0627 = ₹1,00,627. At 10%: A = 10,000(1.10)^30 = 10,000 × 17.4494 = ₹1,74,494. Difference: ₹73,867! Just 2% extra rate multiplies your money by 1.74× instead of 1.01×. Rate matters MUCH MORE over long periods.

slides.title: Aisha's 30-Year Dream
slides.storyContext: Grandma pulls out a chart. 'Let me show you what your ₹10,000 can become if you invest it now and wait patiently.'

points.label: Year 0 (Age 13)
points.text: Invest ₹10,000 in a fixed deposit at 8% per annum

slides.inSimpleWords: Aisha's ₹10,000 investment grows steadily. By the time she's 43, it becomes ₹1,00,626—without her doing anything extra.

image.alt: Aisha's 30-Year Dream — Compound Interest & The Power of Time

slides.title: Aisha Meets Rohan at Age 43
slides.storyContext: Thirty years later, Aisha and Rohan meet. Aisha invested ₹10,000 at 13, earning 8% per annum for 30 years. Rohan invested ₹20,000 at age 25, also at 8%, but only for 18 years. Let's see who won the race.
slides.inSimpleWords: Aisha: ₹10,000 for 30 years at 8% = ₹1,00,626. Rohan: ₹20,000 for 18 years at 8% = ₹100,626 × (1.08)^−12... Let's calculate.

slides.title: The Grand Finale: Aisha vs. Rohan at 43
slides.storyContext: Using the compound interest formula, let's see the final amounts.

example.problem: Aisha: ₹10,000 at age 13, 8% for 30 years (now 43). Rohan: ₹20,000 at age 25, 8% for 18 years (now 43). Who has more?
example.solution: Aisha: A = 10,000(1.08)^30 = ₹1,00,626. Rohan: A = 20,000(1.08)^18 = 20,000 × 3.9960 = ₹79,920. Aisha wins by ₹20,706! Aisha invested half as much but started 12 years earlier—compound interest gave her 26% MORE money. Time beats principal amount.

slides.title: Doubling Time: The Rule of 72
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma teaches Aisha a shortcut: 'If you want to know roughly how long it takes for your money to double, divide 72 by the interest rate.' Aisha: '72 ÷ 8 = 9 years. My money doubles every 9 years?' Mr. Sharma: 'Almost exactly. It's a quick mental math trick.'

points.label: Rule of 72
points.text: Doubling time ≈ 72 ÷ interest rate (%). At 8%, money doubles in ~9 years.

points.label: Why useful?
points.text: Quickly estimate: at 5%, money doubles every 14.4 years. At 10%, every 7.2 years.

points.label: Aisha's money
points.text: ₹10,000 doubles to ₹20,000 in 9 years. Again to ₹40,000 by year 18. Again to ₹80,000 by year 27.

slides.inSimpleWords: Money roughly doubles every 72÷(interest rate) years. This is a quick way to guess how much you'll have without a calculator.

slides.title: The Race: Start Early or Invest More Later?
slides.storyContext: Aisha asks: 'Grandma, what if I start with ₹1,000 at age 13, but my friend Ravi waits and invests ₹5,000 at age 20? Who wins?' Grandma smiles. 'Calculate and see.'

points.label: Scenario A
points.text: Aisha: ₹1,000 at age 13, 8% per annum, invested until age 43 (30 years)

points.label: Scenario B
points.text: Ravi: ₹5,000 at age 20, 8% per annum, invested until age 43 (23 years)

points.label: Question
points.text: Who has more money at age 43? By how much?

example.problem: Aisha: ₹1,000 for 30 years at 8%. Ravi: ₹5,000 for 23 years at 8%. Who has more at age 43?
example.solution: Aisha: A = 1,000(1.08)^30 = ₹10,062.66. Ravi: A = 5,000(1.08)^23 = ₹48,221.23. Ravi has MORE (₹48,221 vs ₹10,062). But if Aisha had invested ₹10,000 instead of ₹1,000, she'd have ₹1,00,626. Starting early matters, but investing more also matters!

slides.inSimpleWords: Starting early gives time an edge, but the amount you invest also matters. Ideally, start early AND invest as much as you can.

image.alt: The Race: Start Early or Invest More Later? — Compound Interest & The Power of Time

slides.title: Aisha's First Withdrawal: A Lesson Learned
slides.storyContext: Year 5: Aisha's bike breaks. She's tempted to withdraw from her ₹14,693 to buy a new one. Grandma stops her. 'If you withdraw now, you lose 25 more years of compound growth. That bike would cost you ₹63,000 in future wealth!' Aisha steps back. She borrows from Grandma instead and repays her. The lesson: early withdrawal is expensive.
slides.inSimpleWords: Don't withdraw early! The money you take out today loses decades of compound growth. The true cost is much higher than the amount withdrawn.

slides.title: The Cost of Early Withdrawal
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma explains the real price of early withdrawals. 'Every year you remove money, you lose compound growth on it forever.'

points.label: The trap
points.text: People think a ₹5,000 withdrawal costs ₹5,000. False. It costs ₹5,000 + all the interest that ₹5,000 would have earned.

points.label: Golden rule
points.text: Once invested, let it grow untouched for 10+ years minimum. The longer, the better.

slides.inSimpleWords: Early withdrawal isn't just about the money you take out—it's about all the compound interest you lose on that money. A ₹1,000 withdrawal today costs you ₹8,000+ tomorrow.

slides.title: Aisha's Legacy: Teaching Her Own Child
slides.storyContext: At 50, Aisha has ₹3 lakh in wealth. Her 12-year-old daughter asks: 'Mummy, can I start saving too?' Aisha smiles. 'Of course. I'll open an account for you. Start small, but start now. By your age 43, you'll be amazed at what compound interest will do.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Aisha becomes a teacher of compound interest, passing wisdom to the next generation.

slides.title: Generational Wealth: Compound Interest Across Decades
slides.storyContext: When parents teach children about compound interest early, wealth can compound across generations. Aisha's daughter starts at 12 instead of 13—that one extra year compounds for decades.

points.label: Aisha at 13, daughter at 12
points.text: Daughter has 1 extra year of compounding compared to Aisha's start.

points.label: By daughter's age 43 (31 years)
points.text: ₹10,000 at 8% = ₹1,23,429 vs Aisha's ₹1,00,626. Extra ₹22,803 from just 1 extra year.

points.label: Generational advantage
points.text: Parents who teach compound interest early give their children exponential wealth advantages.

slides.inSimpleWords: Starting even 1 year earlier adds tens of thousands in wealth by age 43. Teaching children early creates generational wealth.

slides.title: Aisha's Gold Rules
slides.storyContext: As Aisha leaves the bank, Mr. Sharma hands her a card with three rules. 'Follow these, and you'll build real wealth.'

points.label: Rule 1: Start Early
points.text: Time is your best friend. Invest now, even small amounts. Let compound interest do the heavy lifting.

points.label: Rule 2: Choose Safe Returns
points.text: Start with savings accounts and fixed deposits. Safety first, then returns.

points.label: Rule 3: Be Patient
points.text: Don't touch the money. Let it compound. 10–30 years? Perfect. Your money will surprise you.

points.label: Rule 4: Invest Regularly
points.text: Add money every month or year if you can. It speeds up growth exponentially.

points.label: The Formula
points.text: A = P(1 + r/100)^t. Know it. Love it. Let it work for you.

slides.inSimpleWords: Compound interest is free money that grows over time. Start young, choose safe options, be patient, and let time turn small amounts into big wealth.

image.alt: Aisha's Gold Rules — Compound Interest & The Power of Time

subject: Financial Literacy
chapter: Income, Expense & Profit — Running a Small Shop
title: Aarav's Tea Shop Adventure
hook: A teen learns to run a real business and discovers why the money in matters less than the money out.

characters.name: Aarav
characters.role: Class 8 student launching his first tea shop

characters.name: Dadi
characters.role: His grandmother, a savvy business mentor

characters.name: Ravi
characters.role: Local tea supplier, teaches Aarav about costs

slides.title: Income, Expense & Profit — Running a Small Shop

image.alt: Income, Expense & Profit — Running a Small Shop — Income, Expense & Profit — Running a Small Shop

slides.title: Aarav Opens His Tea Shop
slides.storyContext: Aarav's colony has no nearby tea stall. He decides to set up a small tea shop near his apartment building after school. His Dadi encourages him: 'Beta, running a shop teaches you real maths — the numbers that buy milk and bread.' On day one, Aarav writes down every rupee that comes in and goes out. Dadi sits beside him with a notebook.

image.alt: Aarav Opens His Tea Shop — Income, Expense & Profit — Running a Small Shop

slides.title: Day 1: The Alarm Clock Test
slides.storyContext: 4:30 AM. Aarav wakes before school starts. He sets up a small tea corner with a borrowed stove. His first customer—Mrs. Patel from 3C—buys tea for ₹20. Aarav beams. By 7:30 AM, he's sold 25 cups before rushing to school. 'Look, Dadi! I made ₹500!' Dadi asks: 'And how much did you spend on supplies?'
slides.inSimpleWords: Aarav's first morning: sold 25 cups at ₹20 each = ₹500 in income.

slides.title: What is Income? Money That Flows In
slides.storyContext: Aarav makes his first cup of tea. A neighbor buys it for ₹20. Aarav writes: Income = ₹20. By evening, he's sold 25 cups. Total income for day 1: ₹500. Dadi smiles: 'That ₹500 is your income — money customers pay YOU.'

points.label: Income
points.text: All money you receive from selling goods or services.

points.label: Daily income
points.text: Aarav: 25 cups × ₹20 = ₹500

slides.inSimpleWords: Income is the money people give you when they buy what you are selling.

image.alt: What is Income? Money That Flows In — Income, Expense & Profit — Running a Small Shop

slides.title: The Reality Check: Buying Supplies
slides.storyContext: The next morning, Aarav is excited until Dadi asks: 'Beta, where did the tea come from? The milk? The sugar?' Aarav realizes he'd borrowed everything from Dadi. 'I need to buy supplies,' he says sheepishly. They visit Ravi's wholesale shop. Aarav notices the prices: tea leaves ₹150, sugar ₹80, milk ₹200, cups ₹50. He gulps. 'That's... ₹480. More than half my income!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Aarav discovers: making tea costs money! He must buy ingredients to keep selling.

slides.title: What Are Expenses? Money That Goes Out
slides.storyContext: Next morning, Aarav visits Ravi's wholesale shop to buy tea leaves, sugar, and milk. He buys: tea leaves ₹150, sugar ₹80, milk ₹200, cups ₹50. Dadi asks: 'How much did you spend?' Aarav adds: ₹150 + ₹80 + ₹200 + ₹50 = ₹480. Dadi nods: 'That ₹480 is your expense.'

points.label: Expense
points.text: All money you spend to run the business.

slides.inSimpleWords: Expenses are all the costs: what you buy to make and sell your tea.

image.alt: What Are Expenses? Money That Goes Out — Income, Expense & Profit — Running a Small Shop

slides.title: The Profit Formula
slides.storyContext: Aarav's Dadi teaches him a rule: 'Profit = Income − Expense. If you earn ₹500 and spend ₹480, you made ₹20 as profit. That ₹20 is YOURS to keep.' Aarav works it out: ₹500 − ₹480 = ₹20. 'I made profit!' he shouts. Dadi: 'Yes. Next time, can you sell more cups or spend less?'

points.label: Profit
points.text: Money left after subtracting expenses from income.

points.label: Formula
points.text: Profit = Income − Expense

slides.inSimpleWords: Profit is the extra money you keep after paying for everything. If you make ₹100 and spend ₹60, profit is ₹40.

image.alt: The Profit Formula — Income, Expense & Profit — Running a Small Shop

slides.title: Day 2: A Rainy Day Disaster
slides.storyContext: It rains heavily. Aarav has less than 20 customers all morning. He panics. 'I'll only make ₹200 income but I already bought ₹480 in supplies!' Dadi explains: 'This is the real world, beta. Not every day is profitable. Some days you lose money.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Rain reduces customers. Fewer sales = lower income. But expenses stay fixed. Aarav faces his first loss.

slides.title: When Expenses Are Too High: Loss
slides.storyContext: On day 2, it rains heavily. Fewer customers come—only 10 cups sold instead of 25. Income: 10 × ₹20 = ₹200. But Aarav still bought the same supplies: expenses ₹480. He calculates: ₹200 − ₹480 = −₹280. He made a LOSS. Dadi comforts him: 'You spent more than you earned. That's a loss, beta. It happens. Bad weather, fewer buyers, or high costs can cause loss.'

points.label: Loss
points.text: When expenses are greater than income; profit is negative.

points.label: Aarav on a rainy day
points.text: Income ₹200 − Expense ₹480 = Loss of ₹280

points.label: Lesson
points.text: Not every day is profit. A smart shopkeeper plans for slow days.

slides.inSimpleWords: A loss happens when you spend more money than you earn. On a slow day, Aarav spent ₹480 but earned only ₹200, so he lost ₹280.

image.alt: When Expenses Are Too High: Loss — Income, Expense & Profit — Running a Small Shop

slides.title: Fixed vs. Variable Expenses
slides.storyContext: Aarav realizes some costs change every day, and some don't. Ravi explains: 'Tea, milk, sugar change based on how much you sell—those are variable. But rent for your shop corner stays ₹500 every month, no matter how many cups you sell—that's fixed.' Aarav writes: Fixed = ₹500/month (rent). Variable = tea + sugar + milk (changes daily).

points.label: Fixed expenses
points.text: Stay the same every month: rent, electricity, salaries.

points.label: Variable expenses
points.text: Change based on sales: tea, milk, sugar, cups.

points.label: Aarav's shop
points.text: Fixed: ₹500 rent. Variable: tea/milk/sugar per cup sold.

slides.inSimpleWords: Fixed costs are the same every month (like rent). Variable costs go up or down based on how much you sell.

image.alt: Fixed vs. Variable Expenses — Income, Expense & Profit — Running a Small Shop

slides.title: Week 1 Recap: Understanding the Pattern
slides.storyContext: Aarav tracks his numbers over a week and sees the pattern. Good days: 25+ cups, profit ₹20. Rainy days: 10 cups, loss ₹280. Average days: 20 cups, profit ₹0 (break-even). Dadi: 'Now you see why businesses track daily numbers. You must sell enough to cover fixed costs before you even make profit.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Aarav's first week: some days profit, some days loss. The key question: on average, does income exceed all expenses?

slides.title: Full Day Calculation: The Break-Even Day
slides.storyContext: Aarav runs the numbers for a full week. One day, he sells 30 cups and both income and expense balance perfectly. Let's see his exact calculation: 30 cups × ₹20 = ₹600 income. Expenses: tea ₹180, sugar ₹100, milk ₹250, cups ₹60, rent (daily share ₹500/30 days ≈ ₹17). Total: ₹180 + ₹100 + ₹250 + ₹60 + ₹17 = ₹607. Net: ₹600 − ₹607 = −₹7 (small loss). But Aarav sees: 'When I sell 31 cups, I'd break even or make profit!'

example.problem: Aarav sells 30 cups at ₹20 each. Expenses: tea ₹180, sugar ₹100, milk ₹250, cups ₹60, daily rent share ₹17. What is his profit or loss?
example.solution: Income = 30 × ₹20 = ₹600. Expenses = ₹180 + ₹100 + ₹250 + ₹60 + ₹17 = ₹607. Profit/Loss = ₹600 − ₹607 = −₹7 (Loss of ₹7). To break even, Aarav needs to sell at least 31 cups at ₹20 to cover ₹620+ in expenses.

image.alt: Full Day Calculation: The Break-Even Day — Income, Expense & Profit — Running a Small Shop

slides.title: Aarav's Cost-Cutting Idea
slides.storyContext: Aarav notices Ravi's wholesale prices are high. He asks: 'Is there a cheaper tea supplier?' Ravi replies: 'There's one 2 km away, but bulk orders only. If you buy 5 kg instead of 1 kg at a time, it costs ₹120 per kg instead of ₹150.' Aarav realizes: 'If I can reduce my per-cup cost, my profit margin grows!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Smart businesses find ways to cut expenses. Lower cost = higher profit on the same income.

slides.title: Cost per Unit & Profit Margin
slides.storyContext: Aarav calculates: If tea costs ₹150 for 1 kg (enough for 50 cups), that's ₹3 per cup. But at ₹120/kg (buying in bulk), it's ₹2.40 per cup. That ₹0.60 difference per cup adds up. On 30 cups, he saves ₹18. Over a month, that's ₹540 extra profit!

points.label: Cost per unit
points.text: Total ingredient cost ÷ units produced. Lower is better.

points.label: Profit margin
points.text: Selling price − cost per unit. Aarav: ₹20 − ₹3 = ₹17 margin (old). With bulk: ₹20 − ₹2.40 = ₹17.60.

points.label: The advantage
points.text: Bulk buying lets Aarav keep the ₹20 price but earn MORE profit per cup.

slides.inSimpleWords: Smart shopping: buy in bulk to lower your per-unit cost, which instantly raises your profit margin without raising prices.

slides.title: Can Aarav Make ₹1,000 Profit This Month?
slides.storyContext: Dadi asks Aarav: 'If you want to make a profit of ₹1,000 by the end of the month, what should you do? Here's the plan: sell 20 cups daily (his average), at ₹20 per cup, with daily expenses of ₹45 (tea, sugar, milk, cups). Monthly rent is ₹500. Can he hit ₹1,000 profit in a month (30 days)?'

example.problem: Aarav works 30 days. He sells 20 cups/day at ₹20 each, with ₹45 daily variable expense, plus ₹500 monthly rent. What is his profit? Will he reach ₹1,000?
example.solution: Total income = 20 cups/day × ₹20 × 30 days = ₹12,000. Total expenses = (₹45/day × 30 days) + ₹500 rent = ₹1,350 + ₹500 = ₹1,850. Profit = ₹12,000 − ₹1,850 = ₹10,150. YES! Aarav easily beats ₹1,000 profit. To reach his target, he'd only need to work about 3 days!

image.alt: Can Aarav Make ₹1,000 Profit This Month? — Income, Expense & Profit — Running a Small Shop

slides.title: Month 2: Aarav's Expansion Plan
slides.storyContext: With ₹10,000+ in profit from month 1, Aarav wants to grow. He asks Dadi: 'Can I add snacks? Biscuits, samosas?' Dadi: 'Good idea. But calculate: what's the cost, what's the selling price, how many can you sell daily? Do the maths first.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Aarav plans to diversify products. But he must calculate profit margin for each new item before investing.

slides.title: Adding Biscuits to the Menu
slides.storyContext: Aarav researches: biscuit packs cost ₹3 each (wholesale), he'll sell them for ₹10 each. If he sells 15 biscuit packs daily, along with 20 teas, his income increases significantly.

example.problem: Aarav adds biscuits: cost ₹3 each, sells for ₹10. Projects 15 biscuits/day. Plus 20 teas at ₹20 each. Same monthly expenses (₹1,850). What's the new profit for 30 days?
example.solution: Tea income: 20 × ₹20 × 30 = ₹12,000. Biscuit income: 15 × ₹10 × 30 = ₹4,500. Total income = ₹16,500. Additional biscuit expense: 15 × ₹3 × 30 = ₹1,350. Total expenses = ₹1,850 + ₹1,350 = ₹3,200. Profit = ₹16,500 − ₹3,200 = ₹13,300. Adding biscuits increases profit by ₹3,150 monthly!

slides.title: The Danger of Overexpanding
slides.storyContext: Month 3: Aarav is excited and adds samosas (cost ₹8, sells ₹20). But quality drops—rushed prep, angry customers, returns. His samosa costs rise to ₹10 due to complaints and remakes. Sales drop from 10/day to 3/day. Dadi: 'Beta, you expanded too fast. Sometimes less profit spread thin is worse than solid profit on fewer items.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Expansion can backfire. Overextending yourself reduces quality, hurts reputation, and erases profit. Focus on doing fewer things well.

slides.title: Break-Even Analysis: When to Expand?
slides.storyContext: Dadi teaches: 'Before adding a product, calculate the break-even point: how many units must you sell daily just to cover its costs? If you can't reliably hit that, don't add it.'

points.label: Samosa example
points.text: Cost ₹8, sells ₹20 = ₹12 profit/unit. Fixed cost for samosa prep = ₹100/month. Break-even = 100 ÷ 12 ≈ 9 samosas/month ≈ 1/3 daily. Low bar.

points.label: The trap
points.text: Aarav thought he'd sell 10/day (easy). Market was realistic (3/day). He didn't hit break-even, so samosas bled profit.

points.label: Lesson
points.text: Always calculate break-even before launching. If you can't hit it consistently, skip it.

slides.inSimpleWords: Break-even = how many units you must sell to just cover costs. If you can't reliably hit that number, don't sell that product.

slides.title: Aarav's Pivot: Focus & Quality
slides.storyContext: Aarav stops samosas and doubles down on tea + biscuits (his winning combo). He improves tea quality (better leaves, fresh milk, faster service). Within a month, customers double. Dadi: 'You learned: focus beats diversification when you're small. Be the best at what you do.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Aarav refocuses: excellent tea + snacks beat mediocre tea + samosas + bread + juice. Quality > quantity.

slides.title: Pricing Strategy: Cost-Plus vs. Value-Based
slides.storyContext: Month 6: A rich client suggests: 'Aarav, your tea is premium. Charge ₹30 instead of ₹20.' Aarav hesitates. Dadi: 'There are two ways to price. Cost-plus: add a fixed margin to your cost. Value-based: charge what customers think it's worth. You might be underpriced.'

points.label: Cost-Plus
points.text: Your cost ₹5/cup, want 100% margin? Charge ₹10. Simple but leaves money on table.

points.label: Value-Based
points.text: If customers think your tea is worth ₹30 (quality, taste, speed), charge ₹30. Profit margin jumps to ₹25/cup.

points.label: Aarav's test
points.text: Charge ₹30 for premium tea, ₹20 for regular. Premium sells 5/day, regular 15/day. Monthly profit jumps to ₹16,000+.

slides.inSimpleWords: Don't just add costs + profit margin. Charge what customers believe the product is worth. Premium quality commands premium pricing.

slides.title: Should Aarav Hire Help?
slides.storyContext: Aarav's business is booming—30+ customers during morning rush alone. He can't handle it alone. A friend offers to work for ₹300/day (5 days/week). Should Aarav hire?

example.problem: Current: Aarav works 30 days/month, sells 25 cups/day at ₹25 avg, cost ₹5/cup, monthly rent ₹500. New helper: ₹300/day × 5 days × 4 weeks = ₹6,000/month. With helper, Aarav estimates he can sell 40 cups/day (no rush stress). Is hiring profitable?

slides.title: Month 12: Aarav's First Year Review
slides.storyContext: Aarav tallies his first year profit: ₹14,500 × 12 months = ₹1,74,000 (before hiring). He's paid his school fees, bought his parents a small gift, and saved ₹50,000 for year 2. Dadi: 'You're 14, running a ₹15,000/month business. Most adults can't do this. What did you learn?'
slides.inSimpleWords: Aarav's year 1: ₹1,74,000 profit. He learned income, expenses, profit, cost control, pricing, and expansion strategy.

slides.title: Reinvestment vs. Withdrawal: Growth Strategy
slides.storyContext: Dadi asks: 'You have ₹50,000 saved. Will you spend it on a bike, or reinvest in the business?' Aarav thinks: 'If I reinvest, I can expand to a bigger location, hire staff, maybe sell to nearby schools.' Dadi: 'See? Profit → reinvestment → faster profit growth. That's how millionaires are built.'

points.label: Withdrawal strategy
points.text: Take all profit as salary/spending. Business stays small. Aarav earns ₹1,74,000/year forever.

points.label: Reinvestment strategy
points.text: Invest profit back: bigger shop, hiring, inventory. Business grows 30–50%/year. Eventually ₹5,00,000+/year.

points.label: The math
points.text: Year 1: ₹1,74,000 profit. Reinvest ₹50,000 → bigger shop. Year 2: ₹2,50,000 profit. Reinvest ₹75,000. Year 3: ₹4,00,000 profit.

slides.inSimpleWords: Reinvesting profit into business growth is how small shops become enterprises. Withdraw now, or invest now and become wealthy later.

slides.title: Year 2: Aarav's Expansion Decision
slides.storyContext: Aarav has ₹50,000 saved. He's tempted to spend: a new bike, a phone, a trip. But Dadi asks: 'What if you invested ₹40,000 in a second shop location? You could hire a friend to manage it.' Aarav realizes: if he opens location 2, his total profit could double to ₹3,50,000/year within 3 years.
slides.inSimpleWords: Aarav chooses growth: reinvest ₹40,000 into a second location instead of spending on personal items.

slides.title: The Reinvestment Payoff: Aarav's Year 2–5 Growth
slides.storyContext: Aarav reinvests ₹40,000 in a second shop (20 km away, lower rent). By year 2, both shops run: Shop 1 earns ₹15,000/month, Shop 2 earns ₹12,000/month after costs and hiring.

example.problem: Aarav: Year 1 profit ₹1,74,000 (14,500/month). Reinvests ₹40,000 into Shop 2. Shop 2 takes 6 months to break even, then earns ₹12,000/month. By year 2, what's total monthly profit?
example.solution: Shop 1: ₹14,500/month (stable). Shop 2: ₹12,000/month (6 months running). Average year 2: (14,500 × 12) + (12,000 × 6) = ₹1,74,000 + ₹72,000 = ₹2,46,000. Profit increased by ₹72,000 thanks to reinvestment! By year 3, both shops stable = ₹27,000/month × 12 = ₹3,24,000 annual profit—85% growth from year 1.

slides.title: Income, Expense & Profit: Your Key Takeaways

points.text: Income = Money you receive from customers.
Expense = Money you spend on supplies, rent, and running costs.
Profit = Income − Expense (what's left for you).
Loss = When expenses exceed income (Expense > Income).
Fixed expenses stay the same every month; variable expenses change with sales.
To grow profit: increase income (sell more, raise price) or cut expenses (find cheaper suppliers, waste less).

slides.inSimpleWords: To run any business, track what comes in (income) and what goes out (expense). The difference is your profit—or loss if expenses are too high.

subject: Financial Literacy
chapter: Compound Interest & The Power of Time
title: Priya's Piggy Bank Secret
hook: A teen discovers that time + small deposits = big money, thanks to a magical force called compound interest.

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: A Class 8 student saving for her first phone

characters.name: Uncle Raj
characters.role: A bank manager and family friend who teaches Priya about interest

characters.name: Meera
characters.role: Priya's older sister, who saved for years and became rich

slides.title: Compound Interest & The Power of Time

image.alt: Compound Interest & The Power of Time — Compound Interest & The Power of Time

slides.title: Priya's Big Goal
slides.storyContext: Priya wants to buy a new phone costing ₹15,000. Her parents say: 'Save it yourself.' Priya has ₹2,000 in her piggy bank. She's discouraged until her sister Meera shows her a bank statement. 'I put ₹500 in 10 years ago,' Meera says. 'Today I have ₹1,200! The bank paid me interest on my interest.' Priya's eyes light up. Uncle Raj, their bank manager neighbor, invites Priya to his office to show her the secret: compound interest.

image.alt: Priya's Big Goal — Compound Interest & The Power of Time

slides.title: Meera's Success Story
slides.storyContext: Over tea, Meera tells her story. 'I was like you, Priya. At 10, I saved ₹500. For years, I forgot about it—no withdrawals, just letting it grow. At 20, I had ₹1,200. Today at 25, it's ₹1,500+. I barely added anything after the first ₹500, yet it keeps multiplying. That's the magic of time.' Priya: 'So if I save ₹2,000 now at 13, how much will I have at 25?' Meera: 'Let's ask Uncle Raj.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Meera's journey: ₹500 saved at age 10 → ₹1,500+ by age 25, without adding much. Time and compound interest did the heavy work.

slides.title: What is Interest? Rent for Your Money
slides.storyContext: Uncle Raj explains: 'When you give money to a bank, the bank uses it to lend to others and earns money. The bank pays YOU a share of that money—that's interest. It's like rent you earn by letting the bank use your money.' Priya nods. Uncle Raj shows her: 'If you deposit ₹1,000 in the bank for 1 year at 5% interest per year, the bank pays you ₹50. You get back ₹1,050.'

points.label: Interest
points.text: Money the bank pays you for keeping your money with them.

points.label: Interest rate
points.text: Percentage per year. 5% per year = ₹5 for every ₹100.

points.label: Priya's first deposit
points.text: ₹1,000 at 5% interest = ₹50 interest earned in 1 year.

slides.inSimpleWords: Interest is free money the bank gives you for saving with them. It's like paying rent to borrow your money.

image.alt: What is Interest? Rent for Your Money — Compound Interest & The Power of Time

slides.title: Simple Interest: The Slow Way
slides.storyContext: Uncle Raj draws a table on his whiteboard. 'Simple interest is the easy kind—you earn the same interest every year on your original amount.' Year 1: ₹1,000 + (₹1,000 × 5%) = ₹1,050. Year 2: ₹1,000 + (₹1,000 × 5%) + (₹1,000 × 5%) = ₹1,100. Year 3: ₹1,150. 'Always ₹50 each year,' Uncle Raj says. 'The interest never grows because it's only calculated on the original ₹1,000.'

points.label: Simple interest formula
points.text: Interest = Principal × Rate × Time / 100

points.label: Pattern
points.text: Same ₹50 each year, regardless of what happens to the money.

slides.inSimpleWords: Simple interest gives you the same amount of extra money every year. If you earn ₹50 year 1, you earn ₹50 year 2 and year 3 too.

image.alt: Simple Interest: The Slow Way — Compound Interest & The Power of Time

slides.title: Compound Interest: Interest on Your Interest
slides.storyContext: Uncle Raj leans forward excitedly. 'Now, the magic. Compound interest is when interest EARNS interest.' Year 1: ₹1,000 → ₹1,050 (earned ₹50). Year 2: The bank calculates 5% on ₹1,050 (NOT ₹1,000), so you earn ₹52.50. Now you have ₹1,102.50. Year 3: 5% on ₹1,102.50 = ₹55.13. You have ₹1,157.63. Priya's mouth opens: 'I earned interest on the interest I earned?!' Uncle Raj smiles: 'Yes. That's compound interest—it's magic because it compounds, or grows, faster every year.'

points.label: Compound interest
points.text: Interest is calculated on the principal PLUS previously earned interest.

points.label: Year by year
points.text: Year 1: ₹1,050 (₹50 interest). Year 2: ₹1,102.50 (₹52.50 interest). Year 3: ₹1,157.63 (₹55.13 interest).

points.label: Key insight
points.text: The interest amount GROWS each year because it's calculated on a bigger amount.

slides.inSimpleWords: Compound interest is when your interest earns more interest. Your money snowballs and gets bigger, faster.

image.alt: Compound Interest: Interest on Your Interest — Compound Interest & The Power of Time

slides.title: Priya's "Aha!" Moment
slides.storyContext: Priya draws her own table. 'So if I put ₹2,000 in at 6% compound interest, year 1 I get ₹120 interest... Year 2 I get interest on ₹2,120, so that's ₹127.20... Year 3 that's ₹134.84...' Uncle Raj: 'Exactly! The interest grows a little bigger each year. Over 12 years, that compounds to something surprising.' Priya grabs a calculator, eyes shining.
slides.inSimpleWords: Priya calculates her own compound interest growth and sees the magic firsthand.

slides.title: Simple vs. Compound: The Big Difference
slides.storyContext: Uncle Raj draws two lines on a graph. 'Look: after 10 years, simple interest on ₹1,000 at 5% gives you ₹1,500 (₹500 interest). But compound interest gives you ₹1,629 (₹629 interest). Compound is ₹129 more! And after 20 years? Simple: ₹2,000. Compound: ₹2,653. That's ₹653 more!' Priya realizes: 'Compound interest makes a bigger difference the longer you wait!' Uncle Raj nods: 'Exactly. Time is your best friend.'

points.label: 10 years, ₹1,000 at 5%
points.text: Simple: ₹1,500. Compound: ₹1,629. Difference: ₹129.

points.label: 20 years
points.text: Simple: ₹2,000. Compound: ₹2,653. Difference: ₹653.

points.label: The rule
points.text: Longer time + compound interest = exponentially more money.

slides.inSimpleWords: Simple interest grows in a straight line. Compound interest curves up faster and faster. Wait longer, and compound interest pulls way ahead.

image.alt: Simple vs. Compound: The Big Difference — Compound Interest & The Power of Time

slides.title: The Compound Interest Formula
slides.storyContext: Uncle Raj writes the formula on a notepad: A = P(1 + R/100)^T. 'A is your amount after time T. P is what you started with (principal). R is the interest rate. ^T means you multiply by (1 + R/100) for each year.' Priya practices: 'My ₹1,000, 5% per year, 3 years: A = 1000 × (1 + 5/100)^3 = 1000 × (1.05)^3 = 1000 × 1.1576 = ₹1,157.63.' Uncle Raj beams: 'Perfect! You've got it.'

points.label: Formula
points.text: A = P(1 + R/100)^T or A = P(1 + r)^T where r = R/100

points.label: Variables
points.text: A = final amount, P = principal, R = rate (%), T = time (years)

slides.inSimpleWords: Compound interest formula: take your starting money, multiply it by (1 + rate) for each year. The more years, the bigger the multiplier.

image.alt: The Compound Interest Formula — Compound Interest & The Power of Time

slides.title: Priya's Real Problem: Saving for the Phone
slides.storyContext: Priya decides to deposit ₹2,000 in a savings account at 6% interest per year. She wants ₹15,000 in 10 years for a phone. Let's see: Starting amount: ₹2,000. Interest rate: 6% per year. Time: 10 years. Using the formula A = P(1.06)^10, Priya calculates: A = 2000 × (1.06)^10. (1.06)^10 ≈ 1.7908. So A ≈ ₹3,581.60. Priya thinks: 'Hmm, that's only ₹3,581—not ₹15,000 yet. I need to save more monthly, not just use the one deposit!'

example.problem: Priya deposits ₹2,000 in a bank account at 6% compound interest per year. If she doesn't add or withdraw, how much will she have after 10 years?

image.alt: Priya's Real Problem: Saving for the Phone — Compound Interest & The Power of Time

slides.title: The Monthly Saving Strategy
slides.storyContext: Uncle Raj: 'Priya, one lump sum isn't enough to hit ₹15,000. But if you add ₹500 every month AND let compound interest work, you'll get there much faster.' Priya: 'How much faster?' Uncle Raj: 'Let's calculate.'
slides.inSimpleWords: One deposit grows slowly. Regular small deposits plus compound interest = exponential growth.

slides.title: Regular Deposits Compound Too
slides.storyContext: Uncle Raj explains: 'When you deposit ₹500 monthly, each deposit starts earning compound interest immediately. Month 1's ₹500 grows the longest, month 12's deposit grows the shortest. Together, they add up fast.'

points.label: Year 1 strategy
points.text: Deposit ₹500 monthly = ₹6,000 total deposits. Compound interest adds ₹150–₹200 extra.

points.label: Year 2
points.text: Previous balance (₹6,150+) grows by 6%, PLUS new ₹6,000 in deposits = rapid acceleration.

points.label: The magic
points.text: By year 2-3, your interest earnings are bigger than your monthly deposits. Money grows faster.

slides.inSimpleWords: Monthly saving + compound interest is powerful. By year 2–3, you're earning more in interest per month than you're actually saving.

slides.title: The Power of Starting Early: Priya vs. Meera
slides.storyContext: Meera tells Priya: 'I started saving ₹500 per year at age 10. You're 13 now. See the difference?' Let's compare if they each deposited ₹500 one time: Meera (10 years, 5% interest): ₹500 × (1.05)^10 = ₹500 × 1.6289 = ₹814.45. Priya (starting now, 5% interest, same ₹500): ₹500 × (1.05)^7 = ₹500 × 1.4071 = ₹703.55. Meera has ₹111 more, just because she started 3 years earlier! Meera smiles: 'Time is money. Start early, and your money works for you longer.'

example.problem: Meera saved ₹500 at age 10 (now she's 20, so 10 years of growth at 5% per year). Priya starts saving ₹500 now at age 13. If both grow at 5% per year, how much more will Meera have than Priya after 7 more years?
example.solution: Meera: ₹500(1.05)^10 = ₹500 × 1.6289 = ₹814.45. Priya: ₹500(1.05)^7 = ₹500 × 1.4071 = ₹703.55. Difference = ₹814.45 − ₹703.55 = ₹110.90. Meera has ₹110.90 more because she started 3 years earlier. Starting early gives you a huge advantage.

image.alt: The Power of Starting Early: Priya vs. Meera — Compound Interest & The Power of Time

slides.title: Priya's New Plan
slides.storyContext: Armed with compound interest knowledge, Priya opens her own bank account. She deposits ₹2,000 upfront and commits to ₹500 monthly. Uncle Raj: 'In 5 years, you'll have your phone money. In 10 years, you'll have ₹50,000+. By 25, you'll be like your sister—₹1.5 lakh+.' Priya: 'All from ₹2,000 and patience?' Uncle Raj: 'Exactly. Time and consistency are your superpowers.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Priya's new life begins: consistent saving + compound interest = wealth building without stress.

slides.title: Priya's First Review at Year 1
slides.storyContext: Exactly one year later, Priya gets her bank statement. Starting balance: ₹2,000 + (₹500 × 12) = ₹8,000 in deposits. Compound interest earned: ₹240 (about 3% on the average balance). Total: ₹8,240. Priya: 'My money did something without me working! It multiplied by ₹240 just by sitting there!' Uncle Raj: 'Exactly. Year 2, that ₹240 earns interest too.'
slides.inSimpleWords: After 1 year of saving ₹500/month + compound interest, Priya has ₹8,240 from ₹8,000 deposits + ₹240 free interest.

slides.title: Frequency of Compounding Matters
slides.storyContext: Uncle Raj: 'Most bank accounts compound yearly, but some compound quarterly or monthly. The more frequent, the faster your money grows.' Priya: 'So monthly compounding is better than yearly?' Uncle Raj: 'Yes, but the difference is small for modest rates. Over 10 years, it might mean ₹500 extra. But every rupee counts!'

points.label: Annual compounding
points.text: Interest calculated once per year. Most fixed deposits work this way.

points.label: Quarterly compounding
points.text: Interest calculated 4 times per year. Slightly faster growth.

points.label: Monthly compounding
points.text: Interest calculated 12 times per year. Best for long-term savings.

points.label: Rule
points.text: More frequent compounding = faster growth. Small difference, but compound effects matter.

slides.inSimpleWords: More frequent compounding = your money grows faster. Monthly beats yearly, quarterly beats annual. The difference adds up over decades.

slides.title: The Phone Purchase Dilemma
slides.storyContext: Year 2: Priya has ₹16,500 (original deposits + compound interest). A new phone costs only ₹12,000. Priya is tempted. But Uncle Raj asks: 'If you withdraw, how much future growth do you lose?' Priya calculates: '₹4,500 at 6% for 8 more years = ₹7,152. I'd lose ₹7,152 of future wealth just to save ₹12,000 today.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Priya learns: withdrawing early is expensive. The opportunity cost (future compound growth) often exceeds immediate savings.

slides.title: Opportunity Cost & Compound Interest
slides.storyContext: Uncle Raj teaches: 'Every rupee you withdraw today loses ALL its future compound growth. That's the opportunity cost. Sometimes waiting is cheaper than buying today.'

points.label: Opportunity cost
points.text: The future wealth lost when you withdraw money early.

points.label: Priya's example
points.text: Withdraw ₹4,500 today to save money, but lose ₹7,152 of future growth. True cost: ₹3,152 in lost wealth.

points.label: The lesson
points.text: Don't measure cost by what you save today—measure by what you lose tomorrow.

slides.inSimpleWords: Early withdrawal isn't just about the money you take—it's about all the compound growth that money loses. Often not worth it.

slides.title: Two Paths: Phone Today vs. Wealth Tomorrow
slides.storyContext: Priya decides to ask: 'What if I don't buy the phone now, and wait 3 more years?' Using the formula, she calculates her balance at year 5.

example.problem: Priya has ₹16,500 at year 2. She continues ₹500/month deposits for 3 more years at 6% compound interest. By year 5, how much will she have? Compare: buying phone today (₹12,000) vs. waiting.
example.solution: Year 5 balance using the future value of annuity + initial amount: roughly ₹35,000. If she buys the phone at year 2 (₹12,000), she loses ₹12,000 × (1.06)^3 = ₹14,300 of future wealth. Not worth it. By waiting, she'll have ₹35,000 and can buy the phone AND a laptop AND travel.

slides.title: Priya at 25: The Payoff
slides.storyContext: Twelve years later, Priya is 25 years old. She's been saving ₹500/month since age 13, earning 6% compound interest. Let's see her final balance.
slides.inSimpleWords: Twelve years of consistency + compound interest = life-changing wealth.

slides.title: Priya's Wealth at 25: The Grand Total
slides.storyContext: Priya sits with Uncle Raj to review her 12-year journey. Initial deposit: ₹2,000. Monthly deposits: ₹500 × 12 × 12 = ₹72,000 total. Plus starting amount: ₹74,000 in actual deposits. Compound interest earned: significant.

example.problem: Priya: ₹2,000 initial, ₹500/month for 12 years at 6% annual compound interest (annual compounding). Final balance?
example.solution: Using future value of annuity formula: Initial: 2000(1.06)^12 ≈ ₹4,024. Annuity (₹500/month = ₹6,000/year): FV ≈ ₹110,000. Total ≈ ₹1,14,000. Priya turned ₹74,000 of actual saving into ₹1,14,000! The extra ₹40,000 is FREE money from compound interest.

slides.title: Priya's Phone Finally Arrives
slides.storyContext: At age 25, Priya buys her dream phone for ₹15,000. But here's the difference: she buys it with comfort, not stress. She still has ₹99,000 left. Uncle Raj: 'See? By waiting and compounding, the phone didn't hurt your wealth. It's just a small purchase now.' Priya: 'I'm so glad I waited and didn't withdraw early.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Priya's patience paid off. She can now afford the phone without sacrificing her savings or future wealth.

slides.title: Comparing Withdrawals: The Cost of Early Extraction
slides.storyContext: Uncle Raj shows Priya a what-if: 'If you had withdrawn ₹4,500 at year 2 (to buy a phone), what would you have lost?'

points.label: What Priya did
points.text: Kept ₹4,500 invested for 10 more years at 6%. It grew to ₹8,048.

points.label: Cost of withdrawal
points.text: Lost wealth: ₹8,048 − ₹4,500 = ₹3,548 in forgone compound growth.

points.label: The lesson
points.text: Early withdrawal doesn't just cost the money withdrawn—it costs all the future growth too. The true cost is often 1.5−2× the amount withdrawn.

slides.inSimpleWords: Withdrawing ₹4,500 at year 2 would have cost her ₹8,048 in future wealth. True cost = ₹8,048, not ₹4,500.

slides.title: Priya's Next Goal: ₹10 Lakh by 35
slides.storyContext: Now rich by teen standards, Priya sets a new goal: ₹10 lakh by age 35 (in 10 years). She plans to increase her monthly saving to ₹2,000 and invest in higher-yield options (mix of fixed deposits and mutual funds). Uncle Raj: 'At 8% average growth, you might hit ₹15 lakh. Let's see.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Priya's journey doesn't stop. She now uses compound interest as a wealth-building tool deliberately.

slides.title: Scaling Up: From Saver to Investor
slides.storyContext: Priya learns the next tier: she's no longer just saving—she's investing. Different instruments have different risks and returns.

points.label: Savings Account
points.text: 4–5% returns, zero risk. Good for emergency fund only.

points.label: Fixed Deposits
points.text: 6–8% returns, very safe. Core holding for long-term wealth.

points.label: Mutual Funds
points.text: 8–12% average returns, moderate risk. For 10+ year horizons.

points.label: Bonds
points.text: 5–7% returns, low risk, liquid. Diversify across options.

slides.inSimpleWords: As wealth grows, diversify across savings accounts, fixed deposits, mutual funds, and bonds. Different tools for different goals.

slides.title: Priya's ₹10 Lakh Goal: Can She Hit It?
slides.storyContext: At age 25, Priya has ₹1,14,000. She commits ₹2,000/month for 10 years (until age 35) at 8% compound interest. Will she reach ₹10 lakh?

example.problem: Priya: ₹1,14,000 at age 25. Add ₹2,000/month for 10 years at 8% annual compound interest. By age 35, how much?
example.solution: Starting: 1,14,000 × (1.08)^10 ≈ ₹2,46,000. Annuity (₹2,000/month = ₹24,000/year × 10 years): FV ≈ ₹3,60,000. Total ≈ ₹6,06,000. Falls short of ₹10 lakh. Need higher returns (9–10%) or higher monthly saving (₹3,000) to hit ₹10 lakh.

slides.title: Compound Interest & Time: Your Key Takeaways

points.text: Interest is money the bank pays you for savings.
Simple interest stays the same each year; compound interest grows each year.
Compound interest formula: A = P(1 + R/100)^T.
The longer your money sits (higher T), the more compound interest works in your favor.
Start early! 3 extra years can mean hundreds of extra rupees.
Compound interest is called 'magic' because it explodes exponentially—great for savers, dangerous for borrowers.

slides.inSimpleWords: Compound interest is interest on your interest. It grows faster and faster over time. If you start saving early, time becomes your superpower.
